newsitem.title: USA: French courts urged to ban "Larry Flynt" poster.
newsitem.headline: French courts urged to ban "Larry Flynt" poster.

text.p: A French public prosecutor urged courts on Tuesday to ban posters advertising "The People vs Larry Flynt", a Hollywood film about pornography and press freedom, alleging that they offended Christians.

Billboards around France show actor Woody Harrelson, arms outstretched in a position recalling that of Jesus Christ on the cross, wearing only an American flag around his hips against a backdrop of a woman's bikini-clad pelvis.
Prosecutor Therese Gregogna told a Paris court that the poster for the film, by director Milos Forman, was an attack on religious freedom.

Two judges heard separate complaints against the poster from a group of about 30 Roman Catholics, led by two priests, and a right-wing association that aims to combat racism and promote French identity. The judges are to rule on Thursday.
Lawyers for the film's makers Columbia Pictures, a unit of Sony Corp, and the poster firm Dauphin argued that their work was protected by freedom of expression.

"The cross and the crucifix are not the property of only about 30 people," said defence lawyer Magali Thorne. The lawyers argued that the courts had no reason to rule because the Culture Ministry had previously approved the poster.
The controversial film, which won two Academy Award nominations in Los Angeles last week, focuses on the trial of U.S. hard-core pornography publisher Larry Flynt, founder of "Hustler" magazine.

In 1984, a French court banned an advertisment for the film "Ave Maria" which used a semi-naked woman in a crucifix-like pose, on the grounds that it was an intrusion into individual religious convictions.
